title: Harder than stone
hookLine: some stones split and water gushes out, yet some hearts are harder (2:74)

cards: Deep in a limestone cave, you can hear water dripping. It's coming through the ceiling, through solid stone, a drop at a time, and slowly those drops hang icicles of stone from the roof.
Rock seems like the last thing that would let anything through. And yet. Al-Baqarah, verse seventy-four, looks at a rock like that, and then at a human heart.

teach.b: The verse comes straight after the cow.
The people had seen the sign, the dead man brought to life, as verse seventy-three puts it, and the verse says: even after that, your hearts hardened, and became like rocks, or even harder.

Then it does something unexpected. It defends the rocks. Among rocks, it says, are some from which rivers burst out, some that split open so water comes out, and some that fall down out of awe of God.
The comparison isn't fair to the stone. Stone gives way; stone lets water through. These listeners had seen exactly that: a few verses earlier, Musa struck a rock and twelve springs gushed out.
The Arabic for this hardening is qaswah, and the Qur'an uses the word for hearts in other surahs too. It isn't a heart that feels nothing. It's a heart that has seen and stopped responding.
Muslim tradition doesn't treat that as permanent. A report in the Musnad of Ahmad tells of a man who complained to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that his heart had grown hard.

teach.h: FEED THE POOR, TOUCH AN ORPHAN'S HEAD
teach.b: The Prophet told him: if you want your heart to soften, feed the poor, and pass your hand over the head of an orphan. Not a lecture, not a feeling to manufacture: two small acts of tenderness, with the hands.

how: Muslims who feel their hearts growing hard are often advised, following a hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad, to soften them through small acts of care: feeding the poor and showing tenderness to orphans.

o: hardness of heart: having seen, and stopped responding
a heart broken by grief that can't be comforted
the stubborn pride that made Iblis refuse to bow

games.q: stone and heart — tap the pairs.
p: feed the poor, touch an orphan's head

s: the verse says hearts are like rocks, or even harder
and then it defends the rocks: some let rivers burst out.
in Muslim teaching, a hard heart can never soften
the hadith in Ahmad gives two small acts to soften it.
the people in the story had never seen water come from a rock
a few verses earlier, twelve springs gushed from a rock Musa struck.

games.q: a man tells the Prophet his heart has grown hard. what does the Prophet tell him?
o: pray all night until it softens.
feed the poor and pass your hand over an orphan's head.
games.why: two small acts of tenderness, with the hands. the cure for a hard heart, in this hadith, is care for someone else.

practice: Think of someone you've gone hard toward, not someone who harmed you badly, just someone you've stopped responding to, and picture them on an ordinary day, tired, carrying something you can't see.
You don't have to fix anything; just notice whether the stone gives a little.

wordCard.voice: Qaswah. Hardness of heart — al-Baqarah's picture of a heart that has seen and stopped responding, set beside rocks that still let water through. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: hardness of heart; in 2:74, hearts that hardened like rocks.

carryVoice: Your line: even stone lets water through. Hardness isn't permanent. That's day three hundred forty-two.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:72–73 (the slain man, brought to life)
Musnad Ahmad (a man complains of a hard heart; feed the poor, stroke the orphan's head)
